title: Act V, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Scottish thanes (Menteith, Caithness, Angus and Lennox) march to join Malcolm's English power near Birnam Wood. They say Macbeth strongly fortifies Dunsinane; some call him mad, and those he commands 'move only in command, nothing in love.' Angus says Macbeth's title hangs loose about him 'like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief.' They march to give their blood as medicine to purge their sick country.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this play is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “Act V, Scene II,” how does Shakespeare show the tyrant's weakening grip? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the imagery you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Act V, Scene II, how does Shakespeare develop the idea of the tyrant's weakening grip? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the imagery in the scene helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Act V, Scene II develops the idea of the tyrant's weakening grip. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act V, Scene II (where it begins, turns and ends) and its imagery shape the reader's understanding of the tyrant's weakening grip. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act V, Scene II suggests about the tyrant's weakening grip. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's imagery and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses imagery in Act V, Scene II to complicate the reader's understanding of the tyrant's weakening grip. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act V, Scene II within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of the tyrant's weakening grip responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act V, Scene II alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of the tyrant's weakening grip follows or bends those conventions, using the imagery as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act V, Scene II and its treatment of the tyrant's weakening grip. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's imagery and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act V, Scene II as evidence for a larger claim about the tyrant's weakening grip in Macbeth. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act V, Scene II as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of the tyrant's weakening grip. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Macbeth.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: How can you tell when a leader has lost the loyalty of the people around them? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script:
Today's words are revolts, distemper, upbraid, mortified, manhood. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “Now does he feel
His secret murders sticking on his hands;
Now minutely revolts upbraid his faith-breach;
Those he commands move only in command,
Nothing in love: now does he feel his title
Hang loose about him, like a giant’s robe
Upon a dwarfish thief.” In this sentence it means: rebellions. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
